lineages.name: Egypt
lineages.description: Egypt was unified under a single king around 3100 BCE and ruled by native dynasties through the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, separated by periods of division. After Persian and then Macedonian conquest, the Ptolemaic Kingdom ruled from Alexandria until Rome annexed Egypt in 30 BCE.

lineages.name: Mesopotamia
lineages.description: Sumerian city-states such as Uruk, Ur and Lagash arose in southern Mesopotamia and developed cuneiform writing. Sargon of Akkad united the region in the 24th century BCE. Babylon later rose under Hammurabi, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire of Nebuchadnezzar II fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BCE.

lineages.name: Assyria
lineages.description: Assyria, centred on the city of Ashur on the upper Tigris, was a Mesopotamian power from the early second millennium BCE. From 911 BCE the Neo-Assyrian Empire expanded until it reached from western Iran to Egypt. It fell to Babylonian and Median forces after the sack of its capital, Nineveh, in 612 BCE.

lineages.name: Hittites
lineages.description: The Hittites ruled central Anatolia from their capital, Hattusa, from about the 17th century BCE. At their height they rivalled Egypt, fighting it at Kadesh around 1274 BCE and later agreeing one of the earliest recorded peace treaties. The kingdom collapsed around 1180 BCE, in the Late Bronze Age collapse.

lineages.name: Persia
lineages.description: Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire around 550 BCE; it reached from the Aegean to the Indus until Alexander conquered it in 330 BCE. The Parthian and Sasanian empires restored Iranian rule and fought Rome for centuries until the Arab conquest. The Safavids, Afsharids and Qajars ruled Iran from 1501.

lineages.name: Macedon
lineages.description: Philip II made Macedon the leading power in Greece, and his son Alexander conquered the Persian Empire between 334 and 323 BCE, reaching the Indus. His generals divided the empire after his death. The Seleucid Empire, the largest successor, held much of the Near East before Rome annexed its remnant in 63 BCE.

lineages.name: Carthage
lineages.description: Founded by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, traditionally in 814 BCE, Carthage in modern Tunisia built a trading empire across North Africa, western Sicily, Sardinia and southern Iberia. It fought Rome in three Punic Wars, including Hannibal's invasion of Italy, and was destroyed by Rome in 146 BCE.

lineages.name: Rome
lineages.description: Rome grew from a city-state, a republic by tradition from 509 BCE, to rule the whole Mediterranean, and became an empire under Augustus in 27 BCE. It reached its greatest extent under Trajan in 117 CE. The western empire ended in 476; the eastern, Byzantine Empire lasted until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.

lineages.name: Maurya & Gupta
lineages.description: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire around 320 BCE; under Ashoka it covered most of the Indian subcontinent and promoted Buddhism. It collapsed around 185 BCE. The Gupta Empire, from about 320 CE, reunited much of northern India in an era noted for Sanskrit literature, mathematics and astronomy.

lineages.name: China
lineages.description: The Shang, the earliest Chinese dynasty known from its own written records, ruled the Yellow River valley from about 1600 BCE. The Qin unified China in 221 BCE, and dynasties including the Han, Tang, Song, Ming and Qing ruled an imperial state, through periods of division, until the Qing fell in 1912.

lineages.name: Xiongnu
lineages.description: The Xiongnu were a confederation of steppe peoples who, under Modu Chanyu from 209 BCE, built the first great empire of the Mongolian steppe. They forced Han China to pay tribute until Han campaigns and internal splits weakened them; the confederation divided in the 1st century CE.

lineages.name: Tibetan Empire
lineages.description: Songtsen Gampo unified the Tibetan plateau in the early 7th century CE. The Tibetan Empire expanded into Central Asia and western China, contested the Silk Road with the Tang and briefly occupied the Tang capital, Chang'an, in 763. It fragmented after the death of its last emperor, Langdarma, around 842.

lineages.name: Khmer Empire
lineages.description: The Khmer Empire is dated from 802 CE, when Jayavarman II proclaimed himself universal monarch. Ruling from Angkor, it dominated much of mainland South-East Asia and built temple complexes such as Angkor Wat. Angkor declined during the 14th century and was abandoned as the capital after a Siamese attack in 1431.

lineages.name: Caliphate
lineages.description: After Muhammad's death in 632, the Rashidun caliphs conquered the Sasanian Empire and Byzantine Syria and Egypt. The Umayyads, ruling from Damascus from 661, extended the empire from Iberia to Central Asia. The Abbasids took power in 750 and founded Baghdad, which the Mongols sacked in 1258.

lineages.name: Franks
lineages.description: Clovis I united the Franks around 500 CE, founding a Merovingian kingdom that ruled most of Gaul. The Carolingians replaced it in 751; Charlemagne extended the realm across much of western and central Europe and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. His grandsons divided the empire by the Treaty of Verdun in 843.

lineages.name: Holy Roman Empire
lineages.description: The Holy Roman Empire is usually dated from the coronation of Otto I in 962. A decentralised realm of hundreds of principalities, bishoprics and cities under an elected emperor, it covered much of central Europe. Its central authority waned after the Thirty Years' War, and Francis II dissolved it in 1806.

lineages.name: Ghana, Mali & Songhai
lineages.description: The Ghana Empire, flourishing by the 8th century, controlled the trans-Saharan gold trade of the western Sahel. Mali, founded by Sundiata Keita in the 13th century, succeeded it; Mansa Musa's pilgrimage of 1324 made its wealth famous. Songhai, ruling from Gao, grew larger still until Morocco defeated it in 1591.

lineages.name: Seljuks
lineages.description: The Seljuks, a Turkic dynasty from Central Asia, took Baghdad in 1055 and ruled from Central Asia to the Levant. Their victory over Byzantium at Manzikert in 1071 opened Anatolia to Turkic settlement and led to the Byzantine appeal that prompted the First Crusade. The Great Seljuk state broke up in the 12th century.

lineages.name: Mongols
lineages.description: Temujin was proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206 and led conquests across Asia; by the late 13th century the empire reached from Korea to eastern Europe, the largest contiguous land empire in history. From 1260 it split into four khanates: the Yuan in China, the Golden Horde, the Ilkhanate and the Chagatai Khanate.

lineages.name: Timurids & Mughals
lineages.description: Timur, a Turco-Mongol conqueror, built an empire across Central Asia, Iran and Mesopotamia from 1370, ruling from Samarkand; his successors lost most of it by 1507. His descendant Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526. It ruled most of the Indian subcontinent by 1700 and ended after the rebellion of 1857.

lineages.name: Ottoman Empire
lineages.description: Founded by Osman I in north-west Anatolia around 1299, the Ottoman state took Constantinople in 1453 and in the 16th century ruled south-east Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. It lost territory steadily from the late 17th century and was dissolved in 1922, after the First World War.

lineages.name: Kush & Axum
lineages.description: The Kingdom of Kush, in Nubia on the middle Nile, ruled Egypt as its Twenty-fifth Dynasty in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE and later flourished at Meroe. Axum, in the Ethiopian highlands, rose in the 1st century CE as a Red Sea trading power, minted its own coins and adopted Christianity in the 4th century.

lineages.name: Maya
lineages.description: Maya city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul and Copan flourished in the Yucatan Peninsula, Guatemala and Honduras, peaking in the Classic period, about 250 to 900 CE, with temple-cities and a full hieroglyphic script. Many southern cities were abandoned in the 9th century; northern centres such as Chichen Itza continued.

lineages.name: Aztec
lineages.description: The Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan formed in 1428 and came to dominate central Mexico, drawing tribute from hundreds of subject towns. Tenochtitlan, built on an island in Lake Texcoco, was one of the largest cities of its time. Spanish forces and their Indigenous allies conquered it in 1521.

lineages.name: Inca
lineages.description: From their capital, Cusco, the Inca expanded from about 1438 under Pachacuti to rule the Andes from Ecuador to central Chile, linked by an extensive road network. It was the largest state in the Americas before European contact. Spanish forces under Francisco Pizarro captured its emperor, Atahualpa, in 1532.

lineages.name: Spain
lineages.description: The union of Castile and Aragon made Spain a European power, and Columbus's voyage of 1492 began its conquest of the Americas. By the late 16th century it ruled much of the Americas, the Philippines and lands in Europe. Most American colonies won independence by 1826; Cuba and the Philippines were lost in 1898.

lineages.name: Britain
lineages.description: Building on English colonies and trade from the early 1600s, Great Britain (from 1801 the United Kingdom) expanded across North America, India, Australia and Africa and was the dominant naval and commercial power of the 19th century. At its height, around 1920, it covered about a quarter of the world's land.

lineages.name: Russia
lineages.description: Ivan IV was crowned the first Tsar of Russia in 1547 and conquered the khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan. Russian expansion crossed Siberia to reach the Pacific by 1639 and continued into Alaska in the 18th century. Peter the Great proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721; it sold Alaska to the United States in 1867.
